# Colophon {.unnumbered}

This book was written in Quarto, typeset with KOMA-Script's `scrbook`, and built from Markdown sources versioned on Codeberg.

The patterns documented here were first systematised inside a private agent runtime, where the *reckon-db*, *evoq*, *reckon-gateway*, *reckon-proto*, and *reckon-go* libraries grew up together. The libraries are open-source under Apache-2.0. This Codex distills the practice that shaped them. Both will outlive the runtime that birthed them.

The Codex's prose is released under **Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC-BY-SA 4.0)**. Code samples are released under **Apache License 2.0**. The split is deliberate: prose travels through citation, attribution, and translation; code travels through forks and patches. The licences match the travel patterns.

## Acknowledgements

The aggregateless-event-sourcing position presented in Chapter 5 owes its sharpness to Rico Fritzsche's writing and Sara Pellegrini's [dcb.events](https://dcb.events) reference work. The Codex disagrees with their defaults; it does not disagree with their thinking. Greg Young's two decades of CQRS+ES pedagogy taught a generation; Vaughn Vernon's *Implementing Domain-Driven Design* made tactical DDD legible to working developers. The inverted-architecture family was named by Jeffrey Palermo (Onion), articulated by Alistair Cockburn (Hexagonal), and synthesised by Robert C. Martin (Clean Architecture). The Pizza framing in Chapter 3 is what happens when their inversion meets vertical slicing; the slicing tradition itself goes back to Cockburn's use cases and forward through Greg Young's *vertical slice architecture* talks.

The specific name **Pizza Architecture** comes from earlier work at DisComCo (The Distributed Computing Company, [discomco.pl](https://discomco.pl)), whose *Cakes, Onions and Pizzas* presentation first laid out the three-way comparison — Layered (cake), Inverted (onion), Sliced (pizza) — and gave the Pizza its hub-and-spokes diagram with four actor types per spoke. The Codex's Figure 3.1 and the company-model view in Figure 3.2 are descendants of that work; the underlying intellectual lineage is older than this book and deserves naming.

The library worked example in Chapter 11 is generic by design. Any resemblance to a real-world lending system is welcome; borrow the patterns, borrow the schema, borrow the integration facts.

## On the binding

The PDF is built to A5-ish dimensions (170×240mm) to read comfortably on a tablet or in print at a working size. The single-column layout is deliberate; multi-column code blocks are a recipe for unhappy diff views.

## Errata and contributions

Issues, errata, and pull requests at <https://codeberg.org/reckon-db-org/reckon-codex>. The Codex evolves with the stack; substantive changes ship as numbered revisions.
